extracted.subtask_description: Writing straight-news accounts of fires, collisions, explosions, drownings and other accidents for newspapers, emphasizing leads, factual detail, human interest, and organization. Includes examples and notes comparing different wire/press arrangements of the same incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline and source line
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin stories with a dateline giving city and date, followed by a dash and the report (e.g., "New York, Dec. 31. —").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples throughout begin with a clear dateline to place the event in time/place; use this convention to orient readers immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead that states the principal fact(s) concisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with the most newsworthy fact — deaths, injuries, or the critical outcome (e.g., "Spencer Trask ... was killed today by a freight train...").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads here give who/what/where/when/how in one or two sentences so reader immediately understands the gist of the accident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include exact time and immediate circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Report specific times and immediate operational circumstances (e.g., "The train left Philadelphia at 7:58 Saturday morning"; "the explosion happened at 11:30 o'clock").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pin down chronology and setting details to make the narrative credible and precise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify notable victims with biographical/contextual detail
rubrics_metrics.description: When the victim is a prominent person, include identifying biography and relevant affiliations (e.g., Spencer Trask's banking career, Edison association, club memberships).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short biographical sketches explain why a death is newsworthy and provide human/contextual interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe rescue, relief and medical response
rubrics_metrics.description: Detail the immediate emergency actions — alarms, police, ambulances, hospitals, morgues, rescue trains and equipment (e.g., "reserves and all ambulances possible were soon at hand").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including responders and their actions conveys the scale of the incident and the human response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report cause(s) and status of investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Give known or alleged causes and note investigations or inquiries (e.g., "Officials of the road are investigating the cause"; "Failure of a brakeman... is said to have caused the smashup").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between confirmed facts and preliminary or alleged causes; note arrests, inquests, inspectors or pending official probes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid, concrete descriptive detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ concrete imagery and specific physical detail to convey the scene (e.g., "The engine ... toppled over, part of it lying across the trestle work"; "the schooner plunged bow first to the bottom").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive detail helps readers visualize the event; balance vividness with factual accuracy and restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include first-person or eyewitness accounts and quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate survivor statements, direct speech and eyewitness detail when available (e.g., survivor Farrell's description of the lifeboats; Diver Hanson's quoted remark about rescuing men).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eyewitness quotes add immediacy and authority; attribute statements to named sources and preserve exact wording when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report conflicting or multiple accounts and versions
rubrics_metrics.description: When different papers or wire services report the same event, present variations and note differences (explicit note: "should be compared as reports of the same accident given in two New York morning papers").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare arrangements and emphases across dispatches; flag differences in facts, emphasis, or organization rather than forcing them into a single account without attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization/arrangement of material matters
rubrics_metrics.description: There are different ways to arrange identical facts (e.g., telegraphed versions vs. morning-paper arrangements); order of facts and emphasis affects reader impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an arrangement (chronological, thematic, biographical-first, cause-first) suited to the audience and the medium; be aware that wire copy may prioritize different elements than feature-length morning accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite authoritative sources and official statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Quote or attribute information to officials, company spokesmen, inspectors, captains, coroners, or legal authorities when relevant (e.g., mine officials, Supt. Kivlin, captains, State Mine Inspector Louttit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official attribution increases credibility; when officials disagree or withhold comment, state that fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include cargo, property and technical details when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Report on cargo, specie, ship or car construction and other technical/property details that affect causes or consequences (e.g., "$1,000,000 in specie" in a mail car; steel car construction prevented greater loss of life; cargo producing poisonous gases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical details can explain secondary hazards and human outcomes; include them succinctly and accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note environmental and weather conditions as causal or contextual factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Record fog, gale, freezing temperatures and sea conditions that contributed to the accident (e.g., fog at Graves Light, gale in Drake's case, freezing temperatures after sleepers were precipitated into snow banks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weather/contextual conditions often explain why rescues failed or why collisions occurred — include them early if central to the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide background and specifications where useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply vessel, mine or equipment specifications and ownership or operational history when they help understand the incident (e.g., ship tonnage, build year, owner company; mine described as "model" and recently inspected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background can contextualize scale and significance; keep such details brief and relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative chronology and sequence-of-events
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell what happened in a coherent temporal sequence — how events unfolded from origin to aftermath (e.g., derailment sequence, attempts to raise ship, sequence of divers entering the hold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chronological ordering often clarifies cause and effect; use subheads or paragraph breaks to separate phases (incident, rescue, aftermath, investigation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report legal/procedural follow-up and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Include arrests, inquests, remands to coroner, official inquiries and likely investigative authorities (e.g., magistrate actions, U.S. Steamboat Inspectors investigating responsibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers expect to know what legal or administrative steps will follow; report them and their statuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey emotional and social consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe crowds, relatives' reactions, weeping, or public scenes to convey human cost and community impact (e.g., five thousand women and children thronged the mine mouth; wives pleading).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human reactions dramatize the event's toll; use with sensitivity and without sensationalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include safety/technical precautions and anti-patterns when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Mention lapses or ignored precautions that bear on blame or lessons (e.g., divers warned about poisonous gases; brakeman may have failed to flag freight; warnings that hull remained unsafe until ventilated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pointing out known warnings or safety failures helps explain causes and offers preventive lessons; attribute such claims to sources.
